strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: amodal, metric-scale 3D reconstruction during robotic manipulation, where visual evidence is severely occluded exactly when geometry matters for control.

The core idea of combining egocentric RGB, proprioceptive hand geometry, and sparse tactile contacts in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid is well motivated. The use of contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses both during finetuning and sampling is a sensible way to make a generative reconstruction model physically grounded.

The experimental design includes relevant comparisons to Amodal3R and SAM3D, occlusion-stratified metrics, pose-estimation metrics, sensing ablations, tactile-noise ablations, and a real-robot deployment. The ablation results support the main claim that hand geometry and touch help under severe occlusion.

The method is described clearly at the representation and objective level, and the limitations section is candid about calibration, fixed grid resolution, and uncertain generalization to different hands or tactile layouts.
weaknesses: The real-world validation is still quite limited: only five YCB objects are used, there is no real-world pose-estimation evaluation, and the paper does not isolate sim-to-real effects from embodiment transfer, calibration noise, segmentation quality, or tactile localization error. This weakens the strongest claims about practical real-world applicability.

Some claims overstate the evidence. In Table 1, the method does not improve over SAM3D on F@0.02 overall or in most occlusion bins, despite text saying it improves all metrics except the least-occluded regime. In Table 3, the real-world comparison is mixed: the method improves CD/NC/IoU but is worse than SAM3D on F@0.02 and EMD.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Important implementation choices such as model sizes, training schedules, optimizer settings, loss weights, guidance hyperparameters, sampling steps, invalid mesh rates, segmentation source, and runtime/cost are absent or only vaguely specified. The statement that only valid output meshes are evaluated is especially concerning without reporting failure rates.

The comparison to baselines is useful but not fully satisfying. SAM3D and Amodal3R do not use the extra sensing modalities available to the proposed method, while the paper does not include stronger controlled variants such as physics-guidance-only versus learned touch conditioning, contact loss versus non-interpenetration loss, or oracle/estimated masks. This makes it harder to attribute gains precisely.

The approach depends on accurate camera-hand calibration, forward kinematics, visibility/occluder masks, and tactile contact localization. These are acknowledged, but the main evaluation mostly assumes clean synthetic versions of these inputs, so robustness under realistic deployment conditions remains underexplored.

There are several presentation and numerical issues, including likely typos such as SAM3D B3 normal consistency reported as 0.081, grammatical errors, and inconsistent interpretation of table values. These do not invalidate the idea, but they reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: amodal, metric-scale 3D reconstruction during in-hand manipulation, where vision-only methods are genuinely underconstrained by occlusion.

The idea of using proprioception for non-interpenetration constraints and tactile contacts for surface constraints is well motivated, and the shared camera-aligned SDF grid is a reasonable representation for fusing image, hand geometry, and contact cues.
The method is evaluated with several relevant reconstruction and pose metrics, includes comparisons to Amodal3R and SAM3D, and provides ablations for proprioception/touch and tactile noise.
The limitations section is fairly candid about calibration, mask dependence, fixed grid resolution, and uncertain generalization to other hands or tactile layouts.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited. Much of the system is an assembly of existing components: SDF/VAE latent generation, flow matching, TRELLIS/SLat-style refinement, Amodal3R-style mask conditioning, and simple contact/non-interpenetration losses. The paper does not make a strong case that the technical contribution is more than a straightforward multimodal extension.

The comparisons are not fully convincing because the main baselines are vision-only or single-image methods that do not receive the same privileged sensing inputs. The reported gains therefore conflate algorithmic improvement with access to hand pose and touch. Stronger baselines using the same proprioceptive/contact information, or optimization-based physical fitting baselines, are missing.

The real-world evidence is very limited: only five YCB objects are used, apparently with known object meshes for quantitative evaluation, on one robot setup. This is too small to substantiate claims about real-world transfer and cross-embodiment generalization.

The evaluation relies heavily on synthetic grasps and ground-truth-style contacts/masks. The paper assumes accurate visible-object masks, hand masks, camera-hand calibration, and contact localization, but does not evaluate realistic segmentation failures or calibration distributions in a systematic way.

Important experimental details are underspecified for reproducibility, including model sizes, training schedules, loss weights, guidance hyperparameters, inference cost, invalid mesh rates, and exact baseline adaptation/training protocols. The statement that only valid output meshes are considered is concerning without reporting how many outputs are excluded for each method.

The ablations are incomplete. They do not isolate the contribution of physics-guided inference versus training losses, hand SDF conditioning versus non-interpenetration loss, contact representation choices, Stage A versus Stage B, or the value of the SLat/SAM3D refinement path.

Some quantitative results raise questions. For example, SAM3D has a likely erroneous normal-consistency entry of 0.081 for one bin, tactile-noise results sometimes improve over the nominal full model, and F-score is worse than SAM3D despite the claimed reconstruction advantage. These issues weaken confidence in the reported tables.

The paper’s impact for ECCV is unclear because the contribution is highly robotics-specific, depends on instrumented hands and tactile sensors, and the demonstrated visual reconstruction quality remains bounded by a low-resolution 64^3 SDF grid and downstream refinement.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated vision/robotics problem: metric-scale amodal reconstruction during in-hand manipulation, where visual evidence is fundamentally ambiguous and physical interaction signals are highly relevant.

The proposed fusion of egocentric RGB, posed hand geometry from proprioception, and multi-contact tactile cues in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid is technically sensible and well aligned with the stated goal. The contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses, used both during finetuning and inference guidance, are a convincing way to inject physical feasibility into a generative reconstruction pipeline.

The experimental results are encouraging. In simulation, the method improves substantially over Amodal3R and is competitive with or better than SAM3D on most geometry and pose metrics, with especially clear gains under heavier occlusion and in pose estimation.

The real-robot transfer experiment, although limited, is a meaningful positive signal: deploying on a humanoid hand different from the simulated training hands supports the claim that the 3D physical conditioning is not purely hand-specific.

The manuscript is generally clear, with a coherent method description, useful ablations on sensing modalities and tactile noise, and an honest limitations section discussing calibration, mask dependence, grid resolution, and cross-embodiment generalization.
weaknesses: The evidence is still somewhat narrow relative to the breadth of the claims. Most quantitative validation is synthetic, and the real-world evaluation uses only five YCB objects with real counterparts of the simulation test set. This makes the sim-to-real and generalization claims promising but not yet fully established.

The paper would benefit from direct physical-consistency metrics, such as hand-object penetration volume, contact alignment error, or contact satisfaction rate. The core claim is physical plausibility, but most reported metrics are generic reconstruction and pose metrics, with physical validity mainly supported qualitatively.

Some experimental reporting appears inconsistent or needs cleanup. For example, the text claims improvement over SAM3D on all metrics except least-occluded F@0.02, but Table 1 shows the proposed method has lower aggregate F@0.02 than SAM3D. Table A1 also has suspicious repeated values between No-Touch and the full model for several metrics, which weakens confidence in the ablation as presented.

The method depends on fairly strong inputs: accurate hand-camera calibration, forward kinematics, tactile localization, object/hand masks, and a known hand mesh. These are reasonable for a robotics setup, but they limit broader applicability and should be positioned more explicitly as assumptions rather than incidental implementation details.

The novelty is more in integration and conditioning than in a fundamentally new generative architecture: the pipeline builds heavily on existing SDF/VAE, flow-transformer, and SLat/SAM3D-style components. I find the integration valuable, but the paper should be careful not to overstate architectural originality.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main paper: model sizes, training schedules, loss weights, guidance hyperparameters, dataset splits, and real-world trial counts are not all clearly specified. These details matter because performance likely depends strongly on calibration, voxel scale, and guidance tuning.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: metric-scale amodal 3D reconstruction of manipulated objects under severe hand occlusion, where vision-only generative reconstruction is often physically implausible.

The central idea of fusing RGB, proprioceptive hand geometry, and multi-contact tactile cues in a shared camera-aligned SDF grid is compelling and appropriate for robotics-oriented computer vision. The contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses/guidance are simple but meaningful physical constraints.

The method is evaluated against relevant vision-only reconstruction baselines, including Amodal3R and SAM3D, with improvements especially under higher occlusion and for pose metrics. The ablations support the claimed value of proprioception, touch, physics losses, and the distance-based contact representation.

The paper includes a real-robot transfer experiment with an unseen end-effector, which is valuable evidence beyond pure simulation, and it openly discusses calibration/kinematic noise as a practical limitation.
The manuscript is generally clear, with a coherent pipeline description and useful supplementary details about data generation, real-world setup, and additional qualitative results.
weaknesses: The experimental case for broad real-world impact is still limited. The main quantitative evaluation is synthetic, while the real-world evaluation uses only five YCB objects and appears small; no uncertainty, trial counts per object, or statistical analysis are provided.

The comparison protocol raises fairness questions. The proposed method receives proprioception and touch while the main baselines are vision-only; this is appropriate for showing the value of extra sensing, but it makes it harder to isolate algorithmic gains from sensing advantages. A stronger comparison to vision-touch or optimization-based hand-object reconstruction methods is mostly relegated to the supplement and not run on the main dataset.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Many key implementation details are not sufficiently specified in the main paper, including architecture sizes, training schedules, hyperparameters for the physics losses and inference guidance, exact contact extraction/thresholding, and how invalid outputs are handled. The statement that only valid output meshes are considered could bias results if failure rates differ across methods.

The novelty is incremental in parts: the work builds heavily on existing SLat/TRELLIS-style latent flow reconstruction, Amodal3R-style occlusion conditioning, and relatively direct SDF-based physical losses. The contribution is a useful integration, but not a fundamentally new generative model or theory.

The method assumes accurate masks, camera-hand calibration, kinematics, and tactile localization. These assumptions are strong, and the real-world results show sensitivity to misalignment. The approach may be difficult to deploy in less instrumented settings or with dense, deformable, transparent, reflective, or highly concave objects.

Stage B is underdeveloped relative to the claims about final textured reconstruction. The paper focuses on Stage A metrics, while the refinement/texturing component is described as an integration step with limited quantitative evaluation.

The work does not demonstrate downstream manipulation benefits, despite motivating the method through robotic control. Showing improved grasping, insertion, collision avoidance, or pose tracking would substantially strengthen the practical significance.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: amodal 3D reconstruction during hand-object interaction, where vision-only approaches are fundamentally ambiguous and physical interaction signals are highly relevant.

The central idea of fusing RGB, posed hand geometry, and sparse tactile contacts in a shared metric SDF grid is sensible and well motivated for robotic manipulation. The contact-consistency and non-interpenetration losses are technically plausible and directly tied to the stated objective.

The simulation evaluation is reasonably broad in scale, with occlusion-stratified results over 22,680 test images, several standard 3D reconstruction and pose metrics, and ablations for sensing modalities, physics losses, guidance, and input noise.

The method shows consistent gains over vision-only Amodal3R and generally improves over SAM3D in simulation on CD, NC, voxel IoU, EMD, and pose metrics, especially under stronger occlusion. The ablations support the claim that proprioception and touch contribute complementary information.
The paper acknowledges meaningful limitations, especially sensitivity to hand-camera calibration, mask quality, fixed 64^3 grid resolution, and reduced fidelity for thin structures.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. Much of the system is assembled from existing ingredients: TRELLIS/SLat-style latent 3D generation, Amodal3R-style occlusion conditioning, flow matching, SDF autoencoding, and relatively straightforward contact/interpenetration losses. The paper would be stronger if it more clearly isolated what is algorithmically new beyond this combination.

The main physical-grounding claim is not evaluated directly enough. The paper reports standard reconstruction metrics, but does not provide primary quantitative metrics for hand-object interpenetration, contact satisfaction error, contact recall/precision, or physical feasibility, despite these being the core motivation.

The real-world validation is too limited for the strength of the claims. It uses only five YCB objects, apparently real counterparts of objects already used in simulation testing, and the method is only slightly better than SAM3D on CD/NC/voxel IoU while worse on F@0.02 and EMD. This is weak evidence for robust real-world transfer or broad cross-embodiment generalization.

The comparison set is incomplete. There is no strong baseline that uses the same known hand pose and contacts through direct optimization, test-time SDF fitting, or a non-generative fusion method. As a result, it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed generative model versus simply injecting privileged geometric constraints.

The baseline protocol raises concerns. The paper notes that only valid output meshes are considered, but does not report validity/reconstruction rates in the main simulation tables. This can bias comparisons, especially for generative methods. Some baselines also use different amounts of training data and model capacity, making attribution of gains difficult.

Several experimental details needed for reproducibility are missing or under-specified in the main paper: architecture sizes, training schedules, optimizer settings, loss weights, number of flow steps, guidance hyperparameters, mask generation details, and exact real-world ground-truth acquisition for quantitative evaluation.

Stage B is described as mostly an integration step and remains vague. Since the paper presents textured reconstruction as part of the pipeline, the lack of detailed training/evaluation of this stage makes the end-to-end reconstruction claim less convincing.

There are presentation and quality-control issues that reduce confidence: table formatting is hard to read, the SAM3D NC value for B3 appears to be 0.081 and is likely a typo, and the supplement contains visible typos such as 'tryue'. These do not invalidate the idea, but they make the submission feel less polished.

The method relies on strong assumptions that limit applicability: accurate robot kinematics, calibrated camera-hand extrinsics, tactile contact localization, object/hand masks, and a shared grid resolution. These are acknowledged, but the evidence does not show the method remains reliable when these assumptions are substantially violated.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: amodal 3D reconstruction during manipulation, where single-view vision is highly ambiguous and physical interaction cues are genuinely informative. The formulation as metric SDF generation conditioned on RGB, masks, proprioceptive hand geometry, and multi-contact touch is well motivated for robotics and computer vision.

The method is technically coherent. The camera-aligned SDF latent space, Structure-VAE, flow-matching model, contact-consistency loss, non-interpenetration loss, and decoder-based guidance fit together naturally, and the paper explains how these components enforce physical plausibility rather than only visual plausibility.

The empirical evidence is strong enough for acceptance. In simulation, the method substantially improves CD, normal consistency, voxel IoU, EMD, and pose metrics over vision-only baselines, especially under heavy occlusion. The sensing ablations clearly show that proprioception and touch both contribute, and the training/inference ablations support the value of the physics losses.

The real-robot transfer experiment is a valuable part of the paper. Even though limited, testing on a humanoid hand with different morphology from the training end-effectors makes the contribution more convincing than a purely synthetic study.

The paper is mostly clear and well scoped. It includes meaningful limitations on calibration, mask quality, fixed grid resolution, and camera-aligned frames, and the supplementary material adds useful detail on data generation, real-world setup, and comparisons to human-hand reconstruction methods.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation is still relatively narrow: only five YCB objects are used, there is no real-world pose-estimation table, and there is no downstream manipulation or planning evaluation showing that the physically grounded reconstructions improve robot behavior. This limits the evidence for the strongest robotics claims.

The comparisons are not perfectly balanced. SAM3D and Amodal3R are vision-only methods, while the proposed model receives privileged proprioception and touch; the ablations help, but stronger baselines that optimize or fuse contacts at inference would make the case cleaner. The supplementary comparison to human-hand methods is useful but indirect because those methods are not run on the main robot dataset.

Some claims slightly overstate the numbers. For example, Table 1 shows SAM3D has higher F@0.02 overall and in most occlusion bins, while the text says the proposed method improves on all metrics except the least-occluded regime for F@0.02. Table 3 also shows mixed real-world results, with lower F@0.02 and slightly worse EMD than SAM3D.

The method depends on several nontrivial inputs: accurate hand-camera calibration, forward kinematics, object/hand masks, tactile contact localization, and synthetic grasp generation. The noise ablations are helpful, but the real-world failure mode caused by calibration noise suggests deployment may be fragile without careful system calibration.

Reproducibility would benefit from more concrete architectural and training details in the main paper, including model sizes, hyperparameters, compute, sampling settings, tactile thresholding choices, and whether code/data will be released. The pipeline has many stages, and small implementation choices could matter substantially.
